title: The King’s Heart in the LORD’s Hand

verses.text: The king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases.
All a man's ways seem right to him, but the LORD weighs the heart.
To do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice.
Haughty eyes and a proud heart— the guides of the wicked—are sin.
The plans of the diligent bring plenty, as surely as haste leads to poverty.
Making a fortune by a lying tongue is a vanishing mist, a deadly pursuit.
The violence of the wicked will sweep them away because they refuse to do what is just.
The way of a guilty man is crooked, but the conduct of the innocent is upright.
Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife.
The soul of the wicked man craves evil; his neighbor finds no favor in his eyes.
When a mocker is punished, the simple gain wisdom; and when a wise man is instructed, he acquires knowledge.
The Righteous One considers the house of the wicked and brings the wicked to ruin.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, he too shall cry out and receive no answer.
A gift in secret soothes anger, and a covert bribe pacifies great wrath.
Justice executed is a joy to the righteous, but a terror to the workers of iniquity.
The man who strays from the path of understanding will rest in the assembly of the dead.
He who loves pleasure will become poor; the one who loves wine and oil will never be rich.
The wicked become a ransom for the righteous, and the faithless for the upright.
Better to live in the desert than with a contentious and ill-tempered wife.
Precious treasures and oil are in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man consumes them.
He who pursues righteousness and loving devotion finds life, righteousness, and honor.
A wise man scales the city of the mighty and pulls down the stronghold in which they trust.
He who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distress.
Mocker is the name of the proud and arrogant man— of him who acts with excessive pride.
The craving of the slacker kills him because his hands refuse to work.
All day long he covets more, but the righteous give without restraint.
The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable— how much more so when brought with ill intent!
A lying witness will perish, but the man who listens to truth will speak forever.
A wicked man hardens his face, but the upright man makes his way sure.
There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD.
A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD.

context.author: Solomon, named in the heading “The proverbs of Solomon” (10:1). The collection runs from 10:1 to 22:16, about 375 sayings.
context.genre: Wisdom sayings: two-line proverbs, most of them contrasts
context.audience: Anyone learning to live wisely, first the young men of Israel’s court and households
context.mapLabel: JERUSALEM, THE ROYAL COURT OF SOLOMON
context.setting: “The king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases” (v.1). People think their ways are right, but the LORD weighs hearts (v.2), and “to do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice” (v.3). It is better to live on a corner of the roof, or in the desert, than with a quarrelsome wife (vv.9, 19). Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will cry out and not be answered (v.13). The chapter ends with two great reminders: “There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD” (v.30), and “a horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD” (v.31).
context.custom: Farmers cut small channels to lead water to their fields and could turn the stream with a shovel, the picture of v.1. Flat roofs were used for sleeping, drying and storage, and a corner of the roof (v.9) was a cramped place to live. Horses and chariots were the great weapons of ancient armies, and Solomon kept thousands (1 Kings 10:26).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 22 begins with a good name worth more than great riches and then opens “the words of the wise.”
context.timelineBible: God turned the heart of Cyrus king of Persia to let the exiles go home (Ezra 1:1) and the heart of the king of Assyria to help them (Ezra 6:22). “Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7).

translation.meaning: A stream or irrigation channel, turned this way and that.
Right judgment, fair treatment for all.
Deliverance, salvation, victory. It belongs to the LORD.

gospelParallels.note: Judgment without mercy to those who show no mercy (v.13).
There is no authority except from God.

otBackground.note: The LORD moved the heart of Cyrus.
Some trust in chariots, but we trust in the LORD.

overview.summary: The LORD directs even a king’s heart, prefers justice to sacrifice, hears the poor, and gives the victory that no human plan can win.
overview.settingLine: Sayings about the king, justice and God’s rule.

history.t: Water was led to fields in channels.

customs.t: Used for sleeping, storage and prayer.

archaeology.t: Pillared buildings at Megiddo were long thought to be Solomon’s stables; their purpose is debated.
Assyrian kings boasted of their chariots and horses.

overview.discussion: “Victory is of the LORD” (v.31), yet the horse is still prepared for battle. How do I prepare well without trusting in my preparations?
overview.book: The book of Proverbs · 31 chapters. Short sayings and longer poems that teach how to live wisely in God’s world, beginning with the fear of the LORD.
overview.author: Solomon (10:1)
